docs.title: Run them on your computer
docs.text:
1. Get the repository at the release (the notebooks are in it; --branch takes the release's own version of them):

    bash git clone --branch v0.6.3 https://github.com/matteo14c/scarlet-sc cd scarlet-sc

  2. Make a fresh environment with the Python you choose (3.11, 3.12 or 3.13), and activate it. Name the version in the command, so the environment gets that one:

    bash python3.12 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: py -3.12 -m venv .venv, then .venv\Scripts\activate python --version # the version you chose

    With conda instead: conda create -n scarlet python=3.12 and conda activate scarlet.

    Each new terminal starts without the environment: activate it again there first (source .venv/bin/activate from the scarlet-sc folder, or conda activate scarlet).

  3. Install SCARLET with the tutorials extra (the reports, Jupyter, and the widgets of the progress bars):

    bash pip install -e ".[tutorials]"

    To install everything in one go (the reports, the tutorials and the tools to build this documentation): pip install -e ".[tutorials,docs]".

  4. Start Jupyter:

    bash jupyter lab notebooks/

    Jupyter keeps this terminal busy while it runs, and opens a browser tab (if it does not, open the address it prints). Open a notebook and run its cells in order. To stop Jupyter, press Ctrl+C in the terminal.

    Run one notebook at a time: a notebook keeps its memory until it is shut down. Stopping its cells or closing its tab does not free it: close the others first with File → Close and Shut Down Notebook.

    Notebook 03 uses 2 CPUs, which fits a laptop. Its memory, measured with 2 CPUs, SCARLET alone (Jupyter and the browser come on top): in a system monitor's process list, the notebook's own process (Python, or ipykernel) peaks at about 5 GB of resident memory (5.0 GB on a cluster node, 5.3 GB on a laptop); during each transfer two more Python processes run the draws beside it. All of SCARLET's processes together, with the memory they share counted once, peak at about 7.5 GB: about what the system monitor's total memory in use rises by.

The data download themselves on the first run. To download them beforehand, for example on a machine with a better connection: python -m scarlet.datasets --dest notebooks/data (each notebook looks for its files in its own data/ folder). While the repository is private, its release assets need a login: the downloader then uses the GitHub CLI (gh auth login first).

docs.title: assign
docs.text:
assign annotates new cells with a model written by learn. It scores each cell against every cell type of the model and against the background, gives the most likely cell type, tests whether it is clearly better than its competitor, and flags calls that deserve a second look.

scarlet assign --model reference.scarlet --data query.h5ad --output query_annotated.h5ad

import scarlet
calls = scarlet.assign("reference.scarlet", "query.h5ad", "query_annotated.h5ad")   # one row per cell

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• model: a model file (or, in Python, a Model from learn or scarlet.load_model).
  • data: the cells to annotate, an .h5ad file (or an AnnData) of counts, with the same kind of gene names as the reference. Labels in its obs, if any, are ignored. Marker genes the data do not contain are not scored.
  • output: the annotated .h5ad to write: the input as given, with the calls added. In Python, None writes nothing and only returns the calls.

With a model learned with the dense technology preset, assign first reduces the query cells to a comparable number of detected genes exactly as learn did for the reference (the model's targets and its learn seed). The annotated file keeps your input's values. A sparse model reads the data as given.

assign does not match depths: it scores the query at its own depth. For a query of another depth or technology than the reference, use transfer.

docs.title: How a cell is scored
docs.text:
For each cell, SCARLET computes how likely its pattern of detected and undetected marker genes is under every cell type's detection rates and under the background's. Then:

  1. the most likely cell type is the forced call (scarlet_top1);
  2. if the background explains the cell at least as well as that cell type, the cell is refused: scarlet_best is unassigned; otherwise scarlet_best is the forced call;
  3. the best cell type is tested against its competitor, the stronger of the second cell type and the background. The p-values are adjusted over the cells of the run (Benjamini-Hochberg) into scarlet_fdr. When scarlet_fdr is below 0.01 (the advanced option alpha) the call is unique: scarlet_unique holds the cell type; otherwise it is unassigned.

A detection rate measured on few cells cannot be trusted close to 0 or 1, so each cell type's rates are kept away from 0 and 1 by a margin that shrinks as the cell type has more reference cells (the floor). A single marker that a small cell type never showed therefore cannot rule it out on its own.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flags label a call; they do not change it, except the flip test when it refuses.

  • Flip test (scarlet_flip): every cell is also scored without the floor. When the most likely cell type differs between the two scorings, the call depends on genes the candidate cell type never showed in the reference. In plain words: a cell type that never showed a gene in the reference may still have it, SCARLET just saw too few of its cells to know; the floor gives such a gene a small, honest probability. If the cell's top call changes when such genes are treated as almost impossible instead, the call rests on genes the cell type never showed. --flip refuse (the default, for every model) refuses such a cell (scarlet_reason: "the call depends on genes the candidate class never showed"); on the published benchmarks' annotation within a dataset, refusing them never lowered the median F1 of any dataset. --flip flag keeps the call and only marks it in scarlet_flip. (transfer flags by default: across datasets the accuracy of flipped calls varies widely, from 14 % to 90 % right depending on the task.)
  • Positive evidence (scarlet_pe_low): for the forced call, SCARLET counts how many of the cell type's markers the cell detects. The call is flagged when that is fewer than a fifth (rounded down) of the number a cell of that type is expected to detect (the sum of the type's detection rates over its markers). scarlet_pe_note gives the numbers and the typical value among the reference's cells of that type. The call is kept.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text: unique is the stricter call: it leaves more cells unlabelled, and the cells it labels are more reliable. best labels more cells. For every refused cell, the assign view of the report gives the reason: background, ambiguity or flip test. Every column: Reading the output.

docs.title: What can go wrong
docs.text:
• Negative values in the data, a model file that does not load, or a model without scoring statistics (written by another version): see Troubleshooting.
  • Few of the model's markers in the data (different gene identifiers, symbols against Ensembl ids): fewer genes support each call; check that reference and query use the same kind of gene names.

docs.title: learn
docs.text:
learn builds a model from a labelled reference. For each cell type of the reference it finds the marker genes that the type's cells consistently detect and that are rarely detected elsewhere, and stores, for every marker, how often each cell type and the background detect it. The model is one file; assign uses it to annotate new cells.

scarlet learn --reference reference.h5ad --labels cell_type --model reference.scarlet

import scarlet
model = scarlet.learn("reference.h5ad", "cell_type", "reference.scarlet")

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• reference: an .h5ad file (or, in Python, an AnnData object) of counts, cells in rows, genes in columns. SCARLET reads detection: a gene counts as detected in a cell when its value is above 0. Raw counts are the safest input; negative values (batch-corrected, scaled or centred data) stop the run.
  • labels: the obs column with each cell's cell type. Any labels can be used.
  • model: where to write the model file (.scarlet by convention). In Python, None returns the model without writing it.

docs.title: How learn works
docs.text:
In each of 100 rounds, learn draws 100 cells of every cell type (with replacement; a smaller cell type contributes as many cells as it has, drawn with replacement) and ranks the genes for each cell type by how much more often its cells detect them than the cells as a whole. A gene earns a point of stability in a round when it is on the cell type's shortlist of the 150 best-ranked genes. A cell type's markers are its 50 most stable genes. The model stores, for every marker, the detection rate of every cell type and of the background. These numbers are advanced options; the defaults are what the benchmarks used.

Before the marker search, genes on the blocklist are removed. The ranking penalises genes that many cells of the whole reference detect, more strongly with the sparse technology preset than with the dense one.

docs.title: Technology preset
docs.text:
--technology tells SCARLET how dense the data are. Both presets read the same thing from every cell: a gene is detected when its count is above 0. They differ in one setting of the marker search, the background penalty:

preset typical data background penalty sparse droplet data (e.g. 10x), a few hundred to a few thousand genes detected per cell 6 dense plate data (e.g. Smart-seq2, CEL-Seq2), 5,000 or more genes detected per cell 0

The background penalty in plain words. A good marker of a cell type is detected in most of its cells and in few other cells. When SCARLET scores a candidate marker, it multiplies the score by (1 − p)penalty, where p is the share of all the reference's cells that detect the gene. With the sparse preset's 6, a gene detected in 30 % of all cells keeps about an eighth of its score, so markers detected almost only in their own cell type win. On dense data most genes are detected in a large share of all cells, so the same penalty would leave few usable markers; the dense preset's 0 ranks markers on how much more often their own cell type detects them. Neither value is best on every dataset of the published benchmarks, which is why both presets exist.

With auto (the default) learn chooses dense when the reference detects at least 5,000 genes per cell on average, and sparse otherwise. The pre-flight prints the choice and the number it was based on, and the model records it. --technology sparse or --technology dense is used as given. Both presets use 50 markers per cell type ranked on a shortlist of 150.

docs.title: Blocklist
docs.text:
What is on the lists, how auto chooses and how to change them: The blocklist.

Before the marker search, SCARLET keeps known technical and broadly expressed genes (stress, ribosomal, mitochondrial and sex-linked genes, and, unless a label names dividing cells, cell-cycle genes) out of the markers. --blocklist takes:

value what it does auto (default) chooses the bundled human or mouse list from the gene names: mostly upper-case symbols (CD3E) or ENSG ids mean human, mostly capitalised symbols (Cd3e) or ENSMUSG ids mean mouse; it stops with an error when it cannot tell human, mouse the bundled list for that species none no gene is kept out a file path your own tab-separated list with a Symbol and/or ENSG_ID column; a path that does not exist is an error

The pre-flight, the summary and the report say which list was used and why. Genes are matched by Ensembl id or by symbol (case-insensitive). The bundled lists are divided into gene groups; which groups apply is decided from the labels (advanced option blocklist_modules). The summary and the report state whether the cell-cycle genes were blocked and, if not, which labels kept them usable.

docs.title: Unequal class sizes
docs.text: --imbalanced (auto, yes, no) handles references where one cell type holds most of the cells. With auto (the default) SCARLET corrects when the largest cell type holds more than a third of the cells. The pre-flight, the summary and the report say whether it corrected. How the correction works: Advanced options.

docs.text:
option default what it does --gene-col index the var column with the gene names; index uses the var names --seed 42 random seed; the same seed and inputs give the same model --ncpu 1 number of CPU cores; it does not change the result --report off also write the learn report when the model is written --verbosity normal what the command prints: normal (the pre-flight, one progress bar, a closing line), quiet (nothing), full (every step); it does not change the result

The advanced options --n-markers, --marker-shortlist, --n-iterations, --n-cells and --blocklist-modules are also available; the published benchmarks hold at their defaults only.

docs.title: What learn writes
docs.text:
file what it is reference.scarlet (the --model path) the model (members) reference.summary.txt the run's summary, next to the model; also stored inside the model reference_report/ with --report: the learn report

In Python, learn returns the model (a Model): model.identities lists the cell types, model.markers the markers, model.settings what the run resolved. A model file is read back with scarlet.load_model(path).

docs.title: What can go wrong
docs.text:
• The label column is not in obs, the reference does not exist, or the data hold negative values: see Troubleshooting.
  • blocklist auto cannot tell human from mouse: pass --blocklist human, mouse, none or a file.
  • A cell type with few cells (tens or fewer) gets markers from very few cells; the learn report's weak-class table shows how well each cell type is separated.

See also: Reading the output, Advanced options, Troubleshooting.

docs.title: transfer
docs.text:
transfer annotates a query with the labels of a reference of the same species, in one step: it matches the depths of the two, learns on the reference, annotates the query (the first pass), learns again on the query's own stably anchored cells and annotates the query with that model (the refinement), and checks each cell type. The whole transfer is repeated in draws (10 by default), each with its own seed, and each cell's final call is the outcome at least 8 of the 10 draws agree on. It is the command for a query of another depth, protocol or technology than the reference.

scarlet transfer --reference reference.h5ad --labels cell_type --query query.h5ad --output transfer/

import scarlet

if __name__ == "__main__":   # needed in a script when ncpu is above 1; harmless otherwise
    res = scarlet.transfer("reference.h5ad", "cell_type", "query.h5ad", "transfer/", ncpu=4)

In a Python script, call transfer under if __name__ == "__main__": when ncpu is above 1: its draws run in new Python processes, which import the script; without the guard SCARLET stops with a message saying so. Notebooks and the command line need nothing.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• reference: the labelled reference, an .h5ad file (or an AnnData) of counts. Reference cells without a label are not used.
  • labels: the obs column of the reference with the cell types.
  • query: the cells to annotate, an .h5ad file (or an AnnData) of counts, with the same kind of gene names.
  • output: the output folder.

Depth matching reads expression values, so both inputs must be non-negative counts.

docs.title: Origins
docs.text: A query often pools cells of several batches, samples or technologies. --origin-col names a column of the query's obs that says where each cell comes from (never the labels). Depth matching, the refinement and the transfer check are then done separately for each origin. Without it the whole query is one origin, called all.

docs.title: Accurate and quick mode
docs.text:
Depth matching and the marker search are random steps: a different seed thins different detections and draws different cells for the markers, and some cells change call from one seed to another. transfer therefore repeats depth matching, the first pass and the refinement in draws, each with its own seed from --seeds (by default 1, 2, ... up to the number of draws).

  • Accurate mode (the default, --draws 10). Each cell's final call is the consensus of the 10 draws, computed separately for the best and the unique call: the outcome most draws give, where "unassigned" counts as an outcome, is the final call when at least 8 of the 10 draws give it. Otherwise the cell is unassigned with the reason "undetermined across draws". This is a fixed rule: if a cell's two leading outcomes were equally likely in every draw, 8 or more of 10 draws would agree on one of them by chance in about 5.5 % of cells (one-sided p = 0.055). Each output column scarlet_best_agreement / scarlet_unique_agreement says how many draws gave the cell's outcome. With another number of draws, a final call needs 80 % of them, rounded up: 16 of 20, 4 of 5, 2 of 2.
  • Quick mode (--draws 1). The transfer runs once: the same method, one draw. Its calls are that draw's, so there is no consensus, no per-cell agreement (the agreement columns are not written) and no cell is "undetermined across draws". What quick mode gives up: its calls depend on the seed (--seeds 2 gives another draw, and some cells change call), and its stable anchors are that draw's unique calls, so the refinement learns from more, less reliable anchors. On the published benchmarks, quick mode refused far fewer cells of the negative controls (cells of a tissue absent from the reference) than accurate mode after refinement: 42–71 % against 81–100 % (refined best), and the median F1 of a test sample moved by more than 2 points from one seed to another in about three quarters of the samples. It takes a fifth to a quarter of the time with one CPU (see Run time, memory and CPUs).

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: The same inputs, options and seeds give the same output, byte for byte, whatever --ncpu, on the same operating system, Python, maths libraries and CPU type. Results are identical on machines with the same CPU vector instructions; in our tests, a laptop without AVX-512 matched a server with it switched off byte for byte. Where the instructions differ, assign still gives identical calls, and transfer can differ in a few cells (21 of 2,990 in our PBMC example): almost all at the 8-of-10 agreement threshold, and occasionally (1 of the 21) a cell beyond it, because refinement learns from the stable anchors. Another seed list gives comparable results, not the same: on the published benchmarks' transfer tasks, two seed lists (1–10 and 1001–1010) gave the same final call for 77 % to 99.8 % of the cells of a task, and the task's median F1 differed by at most 1.9 points (% unlabelled by at most 4 points). Small references vary more: on test samples whose cell types have only a few hundred reference cells each, the median F1 moved by more than 2 points between the two seed lists in about one sample in five.

docs.title: Depth matching
docs.text:
Reference and query of different depth differ in which genes they detect at all, and SCARLET reads detection. With --depth-match yes (the default), the deeper side is thinned towards the shallower one before the first pass, separately for each origin. The depth of a side is the median number of genes detected per cell, counted on the genes both sides detect; with equal depth nothing is thinned. The thinning fits, across the shared genes, an increasing curve from each gene's mean expression on the deep side to its detection rate on the shallow side, and keeps each detection on the deep side with the probability that brings its gene to the fitted rate. It does not use the labels. Each draw thins with its own seed (per origin), so each draw sees a different thinning.

Thinning affects the first pass only: the refinement learns on the query's own cells, unthinned. When the reference is thinned, one reference model is learned per origin. With depth matching on, each origin is annotated separately. --depth-match no skips this step.

docs.title: Technology preset
docs.text: With --technology auto (the default) the technology preset is chosen from the shallower side: dense only when the reference and every query origin detect at least 5,000 genes per cell on average, sparse otherwise. After depth matching both sides have about the shallower side's density, so this is the density the models see. The pre-flight prints both densities, the gene overlap, the choice and a plain recommendation. --technology sparse or dense is used as given; what the presets do is described in learn.

docs.title: First pass
docs.text: In each draw, the reference is learned and the query annotated, as learn and assign would. The flip test (see assign) is recorded as a flag (--flip flag, the default) and the calls are kept: across datasets the accuracy of flipped calls varies widely; with --flip refuse, flipped cells are refused, cannot be stable anchors and stay refused in that draw's final calls. The consensus of the draws' first-pass calls is written to first_pass.tsv.

docs.title: Refinement
docs.text:
With --refine yes (the default), the first pass's stably called cells teach SCARLET what each cell type looks like in the query itself. Per origin:

  • the stable anchors of a cell type are the cells the first pass called uniquely to that cell type in every draw of the run (in quick mode: the draw's unique calls). They are found once and are the same in every draw;
  • a cell type with at least 3 stable anchors is refined: in each draw SCARLET learns again on the stable anchors of the refined cell types, with their anchor labels and the draw's seed, and annotates the origin's cells with that model. Its background, the profile a cell must fit better than to be called at all, is the detection rate of each gene over all the origin's query cells;
  • a cell type with fewer than 3 stable anchors (zero included) is not refined: in each draw, the cells whose first-pass best call is that cell type keep that draw's first-pass calls; labels.tsv notes "not refined: not anchored stably" in scarlet_refine_note for the cells that kept their first-pass calls in more than half the draws;
  • an origin with fewer than 2 refined cell types is not refined: all its cells keep their first-pass calls in every draw, and labels.tsv notes "origin not refined: fewer than 2 cell types anchored stably";
  • every stable anchor keeps its anchor label in the refined calls (flagged scarlet_stable_anchor in first_pass.tsv and labels.tsv), also in an origin that is not refined.

One round per draw. The refinement does not apply the flip test. The consensus of the draws' refined calls is written to labels.tsv; the stable anchors of every cell type, and whether it was refined, are in transfer_record.json. --refine no makes the first-pass consensus final.

docs.title: The transfer check
docs.text: With --qc yes (the default), SCARLET learns markers on the query with the final calls (cell types with at least 3 cells; at least 2 such cell types per origin) and measures, for each cell type, the share of the reference's markers that the query confirms (share_conserved in qc.tsv). A cell type below 0.2 is flagged doubtful_transfer. The flag points to cell types whose transfer deserves a closer look; it changes no call. How reliable it is: Reading the output.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
option default what it does --origin-col none the query's obs column naming each cell's origin --refine yes refine on the query's own anchors --depth-match yes match the depths of reference and query before the first pass --qc yes the transfer check per cell type --technology auto auto (from the shallower side), sparse or dense --blocklist auto as in learn --imbalanced auto as in learn --gene-col index the var column with the gene names; index uses the var names --draws 10 how many times the transfer is repeated, each time with its own seed; 1 is quick mode --seeds 1,2,... the draws' seeds, separated by commas (by default 1 up to the number of draws) --flip flag the flip test of the first pass: flag (recorded, the calls kept) or refuse --chunk-size 10000 cells scored at a time; lower it to use less memory; it does not change the result --ncpu 1 the draws run side by side, up to this many at a time; it does not change the result --report off also write the transfer report when the run ends --verbosity normal what the command prints: normal (the pre-flight, one progress bar, one line per draw, the result), quiet (nothing), full (every step of every draw); it does not change the result

--seeds is an advanced option, as are --n-markers, --marker-shortlist, --n-iterations, --n-cells, --blocklist-modules and --alpha; the published benchmarks hold at their defaults only.

docs.title: Run time, memory and CPUs
docs.text:
Measured with SCARLET 0.6.3 on two of the published benchmarks' transfer tasks (Abdelaal et al. 2019), one fold each, and on a large query, as a user runs it: the command line, every option at its default (including blocklist auto), --ncpu k on k physical CPU cores (the run confined to them, one thread per core); the whole transfer run, from reading the input files to writing its outputs, without the report, one run each. Peak memory is that of all SCARLET's processes together.

PBMC, 10x v2 → six other protocols: 6,444 reference / 16,710 query cells, about 900 genes detected per cell, sparse preset.

mode --ncpu 1 --ncpu 2 --ncpu 5 --ncpu 10 accurate (10 draws, the default) 82 s, 0.5 GB 51 s, 1.3 GB 28 s, 2.3 GB 25 s, 3.7 GB quick (--draws 1) 16 s, 0.5 GB

A large query: the same PBMC 10x v2 reference → all 65,943 cells of the Zheng 68K dataset: about 550 genes detected per query cell, sparse preset (not a benchmark task).

mode --ncpu 1 --ncpu 2 --ncpu 5 --ncpu 10 accurate (10 draws, the default) 42 s, 1.9 GB 30 s, 2.4 GB 22 s, 3.9 GB 21 s, 5.9 GB quick (--draws 1) 10 s, 1.9 GB

Mouse brain, one region → the other: 8,128 reference / 12,552 query cells, about 11,000 genes detected per cell, dense preset.

mode --ncpu 1 --ncpu 2 --ncpu 5 --ncpu 10 accurate (10 draws, the default) 3.7 min, 3.1 GB 2.2 min, 6.0 GB 71 s, 10.4 GB 52 s, 17.7 GB quick (--draws 1) 41 s, 3.0 GB
  • Deep data need more memory. The brain task has fewer cells than the PBMC task but detects about 12 times as many genes per cell, and needed about 6 times the memory: a deep dataset of brain size needs about 3 GB with one CPU.
  • Accurate mode. With --ncpu k the draws run side by side, up to k at a time; they share the input data and each adds its own working memory: the run gets faster and needs more memory (with 5 CPUs: brain 3.1 times faster with 3.3 times the memory, PBMC 3.2 times faster with 4.1 times the memory). The steps before and after the draws run once, with one CPU: the less time the draws take next to them, the less extra CPUs help (the large query: 1.9 times faster with 10 CPUs). The second CPU added at most the 1-CPU memory plus 0.5 GB, each further CPU at most half the 1-CPU memory plus 1 GB.
  • Quick mode takes a fifth to a quarter of accurate mode's time with one CPU. With one draw, --ncpu only runs steps inside it side by side: little or no faster, and about the same memory as with one CPU.
  • The report is a separate step (scarlet report, or --report), with its own time and memory: with one CPU 49 s and 0.9 GB on the PBMC transfer, 70 s and 1.2 GB on the large query, 1.7 min and 3.7 GB on the brain one, more than the brain transfer itself; --ncpu changes it little.
  • The result does not depend on --ncpu: the same inputs, options and seeds give the same output, byte for byte.

docs.title: Choosing --ncpu
docs.text:
1. Choose a number of CPUs that divides the number of draws: with the default 10 draws, 1, 2, 5 or 10. The draws run in rounds of up to --ncpu at a time, so the run takes about as long as its number of rounds: 5 CPUs run the 10 draws in two rounds, and so do 6 to 9 CPUs, so values between 5 and 10 bring no further speed-up and only add memory (3 or 4 CPUs, in four or three rounds, fall between 2 and 5).
  2. Memory decides how high to go. Take the 1-CPU peak memory M of the table closer to your data, by genes detected per cell first, then by the number of cells. The second CPU added at most M + 0.5 GB and each further CPU at most M ÷ 2 + 1 GB (measured up to 10 CPUs), so k CPUs (k ≥ 2) need at most 2 × M + 0.5 GB + (k − 2) × (M ÷ 2 + 1 GB); take the largest of 1, 2, 5 and 10 that fits in the free memory. For a deep dataset of brain size (M about 3.1 GB): 2 CPUs with 6.7 GB free, 5 with 14.4 GB, 10 with 27 GB (measured: 6.0, 10.4 and 17.7 GB). For PBMC size (M about 0.5 GB): 2 CPUs with 1.5 GB, 5 with 5.3 GB, 10 with 11.5 GB (measured: 1.3, 2.3 and 3.7 GB).
  3. Quick mode needs about the 1-CPU memory whatever --ncpu; extra CPUs save little or no time.
  4. If you also want the report, it needs its own memory (above: up to 4.2 GB on the brain transfer).

If a run stops for lack of memory, lower --ncpu first. In a Python script, call transfer with ncpu above 1 from code under if __name__ == "__main__": (the draws run in new Python processes, which import your script again); in a notebook nothing is needed.

docs.title: Hard transfers
docs.text: Some transfers are hard, and SCARLET then refuses more cells rather than guess: a query of another technology than the reference (for example a plate-based query with a droplet reference, or the reverse), a reference and a query of very different sizes (a reference with a few hundred cells per cell type), and closely related populations (subtypes that differ by few genes). The refused cells are reported with their reason (background, ambiguity, undetermined across draws), and the report shows which cell types they come from.

docs.title: What transfer writes
docs.text:
Everything goes into the output folder:

file what it is first_pass.tsv the consensus of the draws' first-pass calls (the reference model's calls on the query) labels.tsv the final calls: the consensus of the draws' refined calls qc.tsv with --qc yes: the transfer check per origin and cell type transfer_record.json the full record of the run: options, the settings resolved, the pre-flight, the draws and their seeds, depth matching per draw and origin, the refinement per origin, each draw's result, the check, the summary, versions summary.txt the run's summary reference.scarlet (or reference_<origin>.scarlet) the first draw's reference model(s), usable with assign refine_<origin>.scarlet the first draw's refinement model of each refined origin report/ with --report: the transfer report

Columns: Reading the output. In Python, transfer returns a result with reference_models, query_models (the first draw's refinement models, by origin), first_pass, labels, qc and record (the content of transfer_record.json). A refined model can annotate another query:

import scarlet

if __name__ == "__main__":
    res = scarlet.transfer("reference.h5ad", "cell_type", "query.h5ad", "transfer/", origin_col="batch")
    scarlet.assign(res.query_models["batch1"], "query2.h5ad", "query2_annotated.h5ad")

docs.title: What can go wrong
docs.text:
• A label or origin column that is not in obs, negative values, little gene overlap: see Troubleshooting.
  • Query cell types the reference does not have. SCARLET calls only the cell types it learned. A cell of another type is refused when the background explains it at least as well; otherwise it receives the most likely learned cell type. The refinement can also turn cells refused in the first pass into calls; the report shows these cells, and the first-pass calls stay in first_pass.tsv.

See also: Reading the output, Advanced options, Troubleshooting.

docs.text: Generated from the code (tests/test_docs.py); every option is the Python parameter of the same name with the same default (Python reference). yes/no options take yes or no.

Annotate cells with a model.

option values default description --model text required The model: a .scarlet file written by learn; in Python also a Model. --data text required The cells to annotate: an .h5ad file of raw counts (cells x genes); in Python also an AnnData object. --output text required The annotated .h5ad to write (the input with the calls in obs). For each cell type of the reference, SCARLET finds marker genes: genes consistently detected in that cell type and rarely elsewhere. It writes them, with the detection rates it needs to score new cells, to a model file, and writes a plain-language summary of the run next to it. The guide: Learn.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
A report is one self-contained HTML page (open it in any browser; no network or server needed) and, beside it, a bundle of tables (bundle/tables/*.tsv) holding every value the page shows. report reads a finished run's outputs; it changes no call and no output of the run, and shows only values SCARLET computed (UMAPs and the comparison with labels you supply are marked as display only). It needs the report extra: pip install "scarlet-sc[report]".

what you report on the report page a model file (.scarlet), written by learn the learn report: the reference, the markers, and how well the model calls its own reference (cross-validation) learn report an annotated .h5ad, written by assign the assign report: the calls and the refusals of a query without labels assign report a transfer output folder the transfer report: both sides, the first pass and the final calls, refinement, agreement across draws transfer report 
scarlet report reference.scarlet                                   # learn report
scarlet report query_annotated.h5ad --model reference.scarlet      # assign report
scarlet report transfer_out/                                       # transfer report

import scarlet
scarlet.report("reference.scarlet")

learn(..., report=True) and transfer(..., report=True) (--report on the command line) write the report when the run ends.

docs.title: Why a report can take time
docs.text:
• The learn report re-runs SCARLET. Its self-assessment splits the reference into five folds and, for each, learns on the other four and assigns the fold left out: five learns and five assigns. A transfer report includes the learn report of its reference model (its supplement), so it does the same. Switch it off with self_assessment=False (--no-self-assessment) when you only need the rest.
  • The UMAPs are computed for the page, by default twice: on the model's own genes and on all genes. On large data each takes tens of seconds to minutes; umap_all_genes=False (--umap-all-genes no) skips the all-genes one, and umap_cells caps the cells shown (50,000 by default; a seeded subsample above it).

At the default verbosity a report prints one line per fold and one when the page is written.

docs.title: Common to every report
docs.text:
• The page opens on a summary of the result and ends with the provenance: the run's own summary, the SCARLET version, the inputs with the SHA-256 the run recorded (the report checks it against the file it reads and says whether they are the same), the technology preset, the blocklist and its gene groups, and whether the run used the package defaults. When it did not, every option that differs is listed; when one is an advanced option, the report adds that the published benchmarks used the defaults of the advanced options and do not apply to the run.
  • Colours: one fixed colour per cell type in every panel; refused cells are grey. The palette is colour-blind-safe for up to 24 cell types (a footnote on the page says which palette and when it is not).
  • Tables have readable headers; hovering a header shows the column's name in the bundle's TSV and, where useful, what it means. Percentages have one decimal, counts are whole numbers, FDRs are in scientific notation. Wide tables scroll sideways.
  • Refusal reasons: every refused cell has one reason, in the order SCARLET applies its steps: background, then flip test (when the flip test refuses), then ambiguity (the unique call refused while the best call is kept), and in a transfer undetermined across draws. The report stops rather than leave a refusal unexplained.
  • Labels you supply (transfer and assign reports): query_labels (--query-labels) names a column of the query's obs that holds labels you already know, as in the tutorials. The report then adds a section, marked as labels supplied by you, comparing SCARLET's calls with them: the share refused and the median F1 per label on the called cells, the same per label, and a map of labels against calls. SCARLET never reads these labels; without query_labels the section is absent.

docs.title: The UMAPs
docs.text:
Display only: never used for a call. Each UMAP has its own switches:

  • Output (where there are several): which calls colour the cells.
  • View (where there are several): label; margin (learn report: the call's colour darker the larger its margin) or agreement (transfer: darker the more draws agree); ambiguity (the boundary cells in full colour); anchors (transfer: stable anchors outlined); unlabelled (labelled cells faint, refused cells grey with one marker per reason: circle background, diamond ambiguity, x undetermined across draws, triangle flip test).
  • Highlight: one cell type in full colour and the others faint; none by default, so every cell type is in full colour.
  • Space: the genes the UMAP is computed on. By default the model's own genes (its universe: the marker genes SCARLET decides on), read as SCARLET reads them, detected or not, with neighbours by Jaccard distance; the second space is all genes (scanpy's standard steps: normalise, log, highly variable genes, PCA, neighbours). Each title names its space.

Which space to look at. On the model's genes the cells are placed by what SCARLET compares, so cells it cannot tell apart sit together. All genes is the place to look for populations the model lacks: such cells sit with their nearest relative on the model's genes, as SCARLET calls them, and may stand apart on all genes. In one donor's PBMC (a Smart-seq2 reference without natural killer cells, a 10x v2 query with 429 of them), the natural killer cells sit inside the cytotoxic T cells on the model's genes (SCARLET calls 416 of them cytotoxic T), but form their own group at the edge of the T cells on all genes.

Without WebGL in the browser (switched off, or not available), the UMAPs are drawn as SVG on at most 10,000 cells, sampled within each cell type so that small populations stay whole; the title says so.

docs.title: The assign report
docs.text:
Reports · learn report · transfer report

The report of an annotated .h5ad written by assign, for a query without labels: its calls and its refusals.

scarlet report query_annotated.h5ad --model reference.scarlet
scarlet report query_annotated.h5ad --model reference.scarlet --query-labels my_labels   # labels you already know

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
section content Summary cells annotated; the share called and refused, by reason, for the best and the unique call; cell types of the model with no call 1. Depth genes detected per cell, per called cell type 2. UMAP the query by its best or unique calls; highlight and space switches (the UMAPs) 3. Analytics calls per cell type (best solid, unique hatched, the cells left unassigned as a grey bar; the count and share in the hover); refusals by reason 3b. Against labels supplied by the user only with query_labels: the share refused and the median F1 per label on the called cells, per label, and a map of labels against calls 4. Cell type drill-down a cell type's markers and their detection rate in every cell type of the model and in the background; each marker's detection in the model against its detection in the cells called that cell type 5. Flags cell types with no call; flip test and low positive evidence per cell type 6. Provenance the run's summary; the model, the annotated data and its SHA-256, the assign steps, alpha (as the run recorded it), package defaults or not, the UMAP spaces

The refusal reasons are read with the alpha the assign run recorded; another value given to the report is an error.

docs.title: The learn report
docs.text:
Reports · assign report · transfer report

The report of a model file: the reference it was learned on, its markers, and how well the model calls its own reference.

scarlet report reference.scarlet                      # the reference is read from the path the model records
scarlet report reference.scarlet --reference ref.h5ad # when that path is no longer readable

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: section content Summary cell types and reference cells; the cross-validated recall range of the best and unique calls (lowest and highest cell type); the share refused, by reason; the three weakest cell types 1. Depth genes detected per cell, per cell type 2. UMAP the reference: its labels, or the cross-validated best, unique or forced calls (the output switch); highlight and space switches (the UMAPs) 3. Analytics per cell type from the self-assessment: correct, wrong (and to which cell type) and refused by reason, for the forced, best and unique calls 3b. Certainty and boundary cells a UMAP of the cross-validated calls with views label, margin, ambiguity and unlabelled; the boundary map; per reference label the % best correct, % with a unique call, % boundary, % unlabelled by reason, median FDR and margin 4. Cell type drill-down a cell type's markers (highest detection in it first) and their detection rate in every cell type and in the background (bg), in a scrolling box; where its wrong calls went 5. Weak-class flags cell types weakest first by cross-validated best recall, with the evidence: most confused cell type, refused share, cells, a mark for fewer than 50 cells (a reporting convention, not a SCARLET threshold), median genes detected, markers, positive-evidence values; no threshold is applied 6. Per-cell data every reference cell: fold (1 to 5), label, out-of-fold calls, FDR, margin, runner-up, reasons, flags. A Show switch lists the cells worth a look first (wrong, refused, boundary); headers sort; 200 rows shown; the button Download all cells (TSV) builds the whole table in your browser 7. Provenance the run's summary; the model, technology preset, marker sizes, seed, blocklist and gene groups; package defaults or not; the reference and its SHA-256 (as the model recorded it, checked against the file read); the self-assessment settings; the UMAP spaces

docs.title: The self-assessment
docs.text: "How well does this model separate its own cell types?" The reference is split into five folds (n_folds; stratified by label, shuffled with seed). Each fold is assigned by a model learned on the other four, with the model's own recorded options; every reference cell is thus called by a model that never saw it (out-of-fold). It costs one extra learn and assign per fold; self_assessment=False (--no-self-assessment) switches it off.

docs.title: Certainty and the runner-up
docs.text:
• Margin (view margin): the cell type's colour, darker the larger the call's margin, relative to this run: faintest at the 5th percentile of the margin over the run's best calls, full colour at the 95th; the caption gives the two margins. The margins themselves are in the hover and the per-cell table.
  • Ambiguity (view ambiguity): the boundary cells (a best call and no unique call) in full colour, the others faint; seen on the best call (in the unique call they are the unassigned cells).
  • Margin = the log-likelihood of the top cell type minus the larger of the runner-up's and the background's.
  • Runner-up in this report: for a called cell, the cell type ranked second; for a cell refused for background, its top cell type, the one the background beat (its margin is then negative). (In a transfer, the runner-up is the cell type ranked after the top one for every cell: Reading the output.)
  • Boundary cells have a best call but no unique call: SCARLET could not separate the best cell type from the runner-up at alpha. The boundary map counts them by best call × runner-up.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
option default what it does reference none the reference, when the path the model records is no longer readable (in Python also an AnnData) self_assessment yes the cross-validated self-assessment n_folds 5 its folds seed 0 the folds' and the UMAP's seed umap_cells 50000 at most this many cells on the UMAPs umap_all_genes yes also the UMAP on all genes (the second space) alpha 0.01 advanced: the threshold of a unique call in the self-assessment ncpu 1 CPU cores; it does not change the result

Tables of the bundle: colours, depth, self_assessment (per cell), analytics, wrong_to, boundary, certainty_per_identity, umap (x, y on the model's genes; x_all, y_all on all genes), markers, universe, weak_classes.

docs.title: The transfer report
docs.text:
Reports · learn report · assign report

The report of a transfer output folder. A is the reference, B the query; the title names both by their file stems (for example smartseq2_reference → 10xv2_query).

scarlet report transfer_out/                              # reads the reference and query from the recorded paths
scarlet report transfer_out/ --query-labels cell_type     # also compare the calls with labels you know

Three pages: the main page (report.html); what refinement changed (refinement.html), linked from section 6; and the supplement (supplement_A/report.html), the learn report of the transfer's reference model with its self-assessment. If the reference was thinned by depth matching, the supplement says so; its self-assessment learns on the reference as given.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: section content Summary A → B with their cells and cell types; the share of B called (best, unique) and refused by reason; depth matching in one line (which side was thinned, from and to how many detected genes per cell, median over the draws); the draws and the 8-of-10 rule; the transfer check; cell types of A with no call in B 1. Depth genes detected per cell in A and B before depth matching (boxes), and the record's medians on the shared genes before and after matching (after: the median over the draws with their range) 2. UMAPs A by its labels and B side by side. B: output (final best, final unique, first pass best, first pass unique) and view (label, agreement, ambiguity, anchors, unlabelled); both: highlight and space (the UMAPs) 3. Analytics final calls per cell type (best solid, unique hatched, unassigned grey; the count and share in the hover); refusals by reason (background, ambiguity, undetermined across draws, flip test); cell types of A with no call in B 3b. Certainty, boundary cells and refusals the boundary maps (first pass and refined) and the per-identity table 3c. Against labels supplied by the user only with query_labels: for each output, over the cells whose label the model knows, the share refused and the median F1 on the called cells; per label (labels the model does not know listed last, with what their cells were called); a map of labels against the final best calls 4. Cell type drill-down two heatmaps in one gene order and three parts: the markers common to A's model and B's refined model, those only in A's (dropped by refinement), those only in B's (added); left their detection in A's model (A's cells per label), right in B's refined model (B's stable anchors per cell type), with the background column bg. Every value is the model's own estimate, read from its in-class table (in_class.tsv in the model: learn's bootstrap estimate of the share of each cell type's cells detecting each gene, the same estimate the model uses for its markers). A model written before SCARLET 0.6.3 has no such table: the other model's markers are then blank, not a marker of this model in the hover. Each marker's rank in both models (common markers joined by a line); each reference marker's detection in A against the B cells called that cell type; stable anchors 5. Weak-class flags from the reference (the supplement's self-assessment) and from the transfer (ranked by the share of reference markers confirmed, lowest first, with stable anchors and doubtful transfer) 6. What refinement changed cells refused then called, changed cell type, and called then refused (best and unique); the details on their own page, refinement.html: first-pass and refined calls side by side, a map of every change of call (first-pass call against final call) and the list of changes, largest first 7. Agreement across the draws the rule, a histogram of the final calls' agreement (best and unique; at least 8 of 10 in blue, the final call; below in grey, unassigned) and its share by final best call; each draw's own result 8. Per-cell data B's cells counted by how their final call came out (refused, boundary, called below full agreement, called at full agreement); the button Download all cells (TSV) builds the whole table in your browser; Browse the cells opens the table: final and first-pass calls, agreement, reasons, top identity, runner-up (and in how many draws), stable anchor, flags, with a Show switch (the cells worth a look first), headers that sort, 25 rows at a time 9. Provenance the run's summary; both sides and their SHA-256 (as transfer recorded them, checked against the files read); refinement, depth matching, draws and seeds, technology preset, flip test, alpha, blocklist; package defaults or not; the UMAP spaces; depth matching draw by draw

docs.title: Agreement, certainty and anchors
docs.text:
• Agreement of a cell: how many of the draws gave its most frequent outcome (unassigned counts as an outcome). The final call needs at least 8 of 10 draws; below that the cell is unassigned, undetermined across draws. It measures how stable a call is under the random depth thinning and seeds of the draws, not whether it is correct.
  • Agreement (view agreement of B): the call's colour by how many draws agree: faintest at 8 of 10 (the least a final call needs), full at 10 of 10. Quick mode has one draw and no agreement, and no such view.
  • Ambiguity (view ambiguity of B): the boundary cells (a best call and no unique call) in full colour, the others faint; seen on the best calls.
  • Stable anchors (view anchors): the query cells called uniquely to the same cell type in every draw; a cell type with at least 3 is learned again from them (refined).
  • Runner-up: the cell type ranked after the top one, in the most draws (scarlet_runner_up), for every cell.
  • Per identity: cells called best and unique; stable anchors; refined or not, and why; of its best calls, % at full agreement and % boundary; among the cells it ranks first, % unlabelled by reason.
